body.text: Psychology of morbid curiosity and our online fascination with plane crashes

When a Learjet smashed to the ground in Florida early this month, recordings and simulations of the fatal crash quickly generated millions of views as the horrifying content was shared and re-shared across social media.
Wedged between recipe videos and holiday snaps, social media feeds are increasingly packed with confronting content such as disasters, emergencies, crime and death.
Plane crashes, in particular, have a devoted following.
Dedicated TikTok accounts and YouTube channels routinely draw millions of views, alongside entire television shows exploring what happens when things go wrong in the sky.
Nobody watching these videos or researching what has gone wrong is in danger, and no-one can help. So why can't people look away?
In Australia, an enduring plane crash mystery around the disappearance of flight VH-MDX in 1981 continues to fascinate.
Coltan Scrivner, a psychologist and author at Arizona State University, says the answer is in how the brain responds to danger.
"Any kind of large-scale disaster that is something you could find yourself being involved in is particularly interesting to us,"
"Especially if we imagine ourselves having very little control if we were in that situation."
Dr Scrivner specialises in the research of "morbid curiosity", a term that describes a human's natural psychological urge to learn about danger, death and harmful events.
He says people are drawn to stories about plane crashes and other disasters because their brains want to understand perceived danger to make them feel safer.
"It's not because humans are sadists or because they enjoy watching other people who are in danger or harmed," he said.
"It's really because that is a rare instance to learn about something dangerous that's plausible in a very safe setting, say, from your couch."
Why plane crashes?
Dr Scrivner said a plane crash was an example of a popular online fascination, as it's a scenario many people could see themselves in.
"It's also one of the few modes of transportation where we are sort of helpless. We're at the mercy of the pilot and the plane," he said.
"Cars, even buses, you have a little bit more autonomy. You can envision yourself jumping off of a moving bus much more easily than jumping out of a flying plane."
Dr Scrivner said this sense of vulnerability drove people to want to understand the risks vicariously.

"The situations where humans are incredibly trusting and incredibly vulnerable and trying to understand when our vulnerability goes wrong essentially, like a plane crash, is something that we're incredibly interested in finding out about."

There are countless stories of plane disasters that have garnered global attention, including the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 in 2014 and, more recently, Air India flight 171 that crashed 32 seconds after take-off, leaving only one survivor.
In Australia, the 45-year mystery of what happened to flight VH-MDX, which vanished over the Barrington Tops in 1981 with five men on board, continues to intrigue.
It is the only civilian plane to crash over mainland Australia with no trace ever found.
Dozens of people with no direct connection to those on board have dedicated countless hours searching for the plane's remnants and researching what went wrong.
Glenn Strkalj has dedicated years to searching for the plane and told the Expanse podcast it's like a problem to solve.
" We'd like to close out some answers and questions that we have regarding some of the unknowns and whether we could potentially obtain more information from the wreck site," he said.
"That next level of inquisitiveness comes into it."
There's even a pilot in New Zealand, Gavin Grimmer, who has spent years researching the plane's disappearance from afar.
Dr Scrivner said this inquisitiveness about an event like a plane crash was normal.
"Learning about something good firsthand is a great way to learn about it. Learning about something bad firsthand is a bad way to learn about it," Dr Scrivner said.
"So learning about something bad second-hand is a much more attractive thing to our mind."
The popularity of true crime
Dr Scrivner believes morbid curiosity also explains people's fascination with true crime documentaries and news.
He said it's important to stress that people's interest in disasters and crime is normal, driven by psychological impulses we all have.
"One common misconception ... is that, you know, being interested in this kind of thing is sort of a sign of psychological sickness or something," he said.
"But it's a very normal human, I would say even a normal animal thing to do, right?
"Other animals are also interested in situations that are dangerous. The difference in humans is that we have a really broad set of tools for communicating that information."
Research suggests that women are the largest demographic consuming true crime content, often focusing on distressing and brutal cases.
Dr Scrivner suggests that may be because they are looking to arm themselves with information.
"Our minds are kind of tuned to seek out that — preparatory information for situations that we would otherwise find ourselves completely incapable of handling," he said.
"We want to gather all the information we can about what could possibly precipitate a situation like this so that we can avoid it, if possible."
